newsitem.title: UK: Aluminium market seen tightening through 2001 - Bird.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium market seen tightening through 2001 - Bird.

text.p: The supply-demand balance in aluminium will soon become tight, increasing until the turn of the millenium, pushing up prices, industry specialists Anthony Bird and Associates said.

"At the beginning of the year, capacity utilisation in the West was 93 percent and stocks of metal in the supply system which are surplus to normal operating requirements are only about 800,000 tonnes," Bird's latest quarterly analysis said.
"This is a supply system with very little slack in it to meet any marked upturn in demand," the report added.
The situation stems from a strategy of underinvestment by aluminium firms sparked by serious oversupply problems in the 1970s and early 1980s.
"But they have continued this strategy of underinvestment into the 1990s, even though the underlying rate of growth of demand has accelerated," Bird said.

Currently, Western primary aluminium consumption is growing on average about 1.5 times as rapidly as industrial production. Aluminium demand growth in the West is expected to be four percent each year from 1990 to 2007, the report added.
Aluminium firms are studying 29 new possible smelter projects in addition to those under construction now, but few are being pursued with much energy, Bird said.
"If we apply heavy discount factors as appropriate, it turns out the rate of growth of planned smelter capacity over the next few years in the West is a very modest 1.4 percent a year," Bird said.
"We think that a tight market is in prospect for 1998 and that the supply-demand balance will grow very tight indeed in 1999 and 2000."

The market will see a jump in prices, which are expected to average $1,828 per tonne this year, said Bird, using a physical price in the United States based on the Metals Week system of adding a physical premium to LME cash.
Prices are expected to average $2,286 in 1998 and range from $2,750 to $3,050 during the following two years. --Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
